source_text: Prudenter ergo, cum de Adam loqueretur, nominavit unum peccatum, quod voluit intellegi formam praevaricationis fuisse; ideo, inquam, unum et non multa memoravit, quia sciebat unum tantum Adae peccatum in legis historia contineri. Gratiam vero ex multis delictis in iustificationem imbutos a se laudavit emittere, ne beneficii pauperis suspicio nasceretur; et si dixisset: Gratia ex uno in iustificationem, non tam omnia videretur abolere quam singula. Quod ergo praemisit unum peccatum, fidem servavit historiae; quod subdidit: Ex multis gratia in iustificationem, munificentiam mysterii commendavit et copiam.
pass_a_gloss: Prudently therefore, when he was speaking about Adam, he named one sin, which he wanted to be understood to have been a form of transgression; for this reason, I say, he commemorated one and not many, because he knew that only one sin of Adam is contained in the history of the law. But he praised grace for sending out those imbued by it into justification from many offenses, lest a suspicion of a poor benefit be born; and if he had said: Grace from one into justification, he would seem not so much to abolish all as singles. What therefore he sent ahead as one sin, he kept the faith of the history; what he subjoined: From many grace into justification, he commended the munificence of the mystery and the plenty.

lemmas.lexica: LS praevaricatio; Blaise Adam's transgression as example
LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: Wisely, therefore, when speaking of Adam, he named one sin, which he intended to be understood as a model of transgression. He mentioned one, I repeat, and not many, because he knew that only one sin of Adam is recorded in the law’s history. But he praised grace for sending those it initiates out into justification from many offenses, to prevent any suspicion of a meager benefit. If he had said, ‘Grace is from one offense to justification,’ it might have seemed to abolish individual sins rather than all sins. Thus, by first mentioning one sin he remained faithful to the history; by adding, ‘Grace is from many offenses to justification,’ he commended the sacrament’s generosity and abundance (Romans 5:16).

choices.why: Adam's act of crossing the command; Julian's example of sin, not a transmitted nature.
Paul's delictum of the one man; an act, not a nature.
